speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. Si. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ERECTION OF STATUE ON PARLIAMENT HILL
speechtext:
Hon. members, I believe, will be interested in a report on the progress made since I announced on February 5 that it is the intention of the government to recommend the erection of a statue to mark the services to Canada of the late Sir Robert Borden.
Since that time the matter has been carefully considered by the board of trustees of the National Gallery of Canada and I now have their recommendation, which has been concurred in by the government.
It is proposed to have the design selected as the result of a competition which will be open to sculptors normally resident in Canada. The base is to be of stone or granite and the figure, which is to be standing, is to be of bronze. The dimensions of the statue will toe similar to those of the statue to the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier on the grounds of the parliament buildings. The announcement of the competition is being made immediately and it is hoped that the closing date for designs may be set early in the summer so that the statue may be completed in time for unveiling next year on the 100th anniversary of Sir Robert Borden's birth. The cost is estimated at between $40,000 and $50,000.
The winner of the competition, of course, will be awarded the contract for the statue, but in order to promote interest among sculptors and also so that not all but one will spend time on producing a design at a loss to themselves, it is proposed to make six additional cash awards of $300 to the six sculptors whose designs are considered most meritorious following the winning design.
Steps will be taken to announce the competition widely through Canada and I am hopeful that the designs which will be produced will be of high quality and in keeping with the service rendered to Canada by the man who was prime minister during the difficult days of world war I.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday last the
hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) inquired about a report that had been published in the newspapers attributing to the Canadian ambassador to Colombia a statement that Canada might eventually join the PanAmerican Union if the union tendered such an invitation, and he inquired whether there had been any change in the government's policy. The answer will be found in Hansard of Friday, March 27, at page 3341. He then

Newfoundland
asked whether the department would inquire of the ambassador whether this report of the statement attributed to him was correct or not, and I told him that an inquiry had already been sent to the ambassador. The department received on Saturday the answer which I would have communicated yesterday had the hon. member been in his seat. It is as follows:
Bid not say Canada would accept invitation if tendered but question of pressmen was whether partnership in commonwealth was obstacle to joining because of link to crown and reply was that there existed no constitutional or juridical impediment since Canada as independent nation is free to determine own policy regarding membership in any international or regional organization as shown by membership in many such. Definitely did not, repeat not, say that Canada might eventually join if invited. Local press correctly interpreted sense of my words as clippings to be airmailed shortly will bear out and I cannot understand how different meaning was conveyed to Canadian newspapers unless press news agency misunderstood, because whole press conference in Spanish without interpreters. Incidentally press conference was great success eliciting in all papers testimony of most gratifying liking and admiration for Canada. Colombians all wonderfully friendly.

subtopic: FOURTH ANNIVERSARY OF ENTRANCE INTO CONFEDERATION
speechtext:
As I have not been here on any other occasion when this anniversary came around, I think I may also claim the indulgence of the house. If I may be permitted to do so, I should like to make a personal reference. As some hon. members may know, 1 was in the party opposed to confederation. Although I was

not free and in politics at the time but was in the government service, I did not wish to see confederation. Four years ago today I was in the city of London, England, and I bought all the morning newspapers to see what they had to say about what was taking place. Most of them had nothing to say whatever; there were two or three references to the act of union that was being consummated, and one expressed regret and said that it was too bad to see an old dominion going out of existence.
I felt extremely sad at that time, and there were many others in Newfoundland who felt as I did. Since that time I have come to regard the situation' in a different light. After having been proud of our almost continuous association with England since 1497, and having been boastful of the fact that we were England's oldest colony, to be cut adrift like that without a word hurt a great many of us. But now we see that England had her own problems and that probably what she was doing then was being cruel in order to be kind. On this side of the water there was rejoicing and I personally received, from friends I had made here when I was for four years at the University of Toronto, an extremely cordial welcome into the union which I did not appreciate then as much as I have appreciated it since. Time has dissipated to a great extent the sadness which I then felt, and I am inclined to think that the majority of people who felt as I did in 1949 feel much as I do now. We were inclined to think then that it was a forced union, and I am not inclined to differ from that opinion yet; but still I believe it was to our mutual advantage.
I have heard here many nice references to our country, and I appreciate them greatly. It is extremely interesting and nice to hear the glowing accounts which visitors to Newfoundland bring back as a result of their visits. The latest one I heard was that of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier); and I am glad to know that in the city of St. John's, where the majority of members are of a political persuasion different from his own-

Mr. Speaker, I know of no
move toward higher duties against Canadian metals. I read the article in the New York Times but such information as I have received does not indicate that any move of the kind is contemplated.
Prices for metals are still satisfactory, except for marginal producers. Lead and zinc have been much higher in price, but today I think the price can be considered to be normal, having in mind costs of production. The price of copper, of course, is extremely high. speechtext: the third reading of Bill No. 107, to amend the Post Office Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTRACTS FOR CONVEYING MAIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall not delay the house very long but

Post Office Act
this is an important bill which affects many people all over Canada. I had some remarks to make on the second reading of the bill and I asked that it not be rushed to the extent it was being rushed at the end of the last sitting. I give my support to this bill to amend the Post Office Act. As I stated on the second reading, I was not a member of the special committee and I have not full information as to the evidence submitted. I am disappointed that there was no representative of the mail couriers asked to be present. I certainly expected that there would be someone representing the mail couriers of Nova Scotia.
I am in agreement with the viewpoint that has been expressed, that many of these couriers have been underpaid for their services and the cost of their equipment. This condition has prevailed over many years, but nevertheless on the whole excellent service has been rendered. Some increase was granted in the war years, but many of the couriers were not advised and had no opportunity of applying for the increase. Only favoured persons received an increase on their contracts at that time.
This bill puts extensive authority in the hands of the minister, the deputy minister and the officials of the department. I am satisfied that the officials are capable, want to do their best in giving good service and will not allow partisan interference to undermine their efforts if they can prevent it. We have the personal assurance of the minister, and I assume that this will apply to his successors, that he will not allow partisanship to dominate the department. It is on this assurance that I give support to the bill.
I do not want the house to think that I believe that this has always been the case, that there has been no partisanship even in recent years. Couriers and the staff are entitled to their political opinions provided the service is not interfered with. To show that I am not gullible I am going to recount the details of one instance in my county during the last two years.
The contract for the mail service on Oxford K. R. No. 2 was for $700 per annum and expired on December 31, 1952. It was held by Mr. George E. Wood. This contractor was not satisfied and he gave three months' notice of the termination of his contract. New tenders were called but only one offer was received from the same contractor, Mr. George E. Wood, for $1,200. The Post Office Department considered this to be too high and refused to renew at that price.
The Post Office Department obtained a revised offer from Mr. Wood of $1,100, but 
considered that price too great also. A tender was then obtained from Leigh L. Smith at $80 per month or $960 per year. Mr. Smith had previously held the contract and had never missed a trip during this entire period. Instructions were issued on December 10, 1951, that the department was awarding the contract for one year to Leigh L. Smith at $960 per year. Mr. Smith was advised accordingly by an official of the Post Office Department.
I asked for the file which the minister sent to me. This file contained a copy of a letter dated December 3, 1951, signed by G. Herring, director of communications and addressed to C. E. Bragg, Collingwood, Nova Scotia. This reads:
In connection with the invitation of tenders for the conveyance of mails over Oxford rural route No. 2, I wish to inform you that the department intends to award a one-year contract to Mr. Leigh L. Smith, Box 128, Oxford, who submitted the lowest offer at the rate of $960 per annum.
Everything was in order up to that point and was most creditable to the minister, to the deputy minister and to the officials of the department. But partisanship, discrimination and interference then took charge. There was another letter on this file from the Department of Resources and Development. I am not going to accuse the minister of anything, but this letter was on the file; and it reads as follows:
Minister of Resources and Development
Ottawa, February 11, 1952
Mr. George Herring,
Director of Communications,
Post Office Department,
Langevin Block,
Ottawa.
Re: Oxford Rural Route No. 2,
Mr. George Wood, Oxford, N.S.
Dear Mr. Herring:
In accordance with our telephone conversation of this afternoon with respect to the recommendation of a carrier for the above-mentioned route, I would like on behalf of Mr. Elmer Bragg, of Amherst, to recommend that the contract for this service be continued by Mr. Wood of Oxford, who has had 12 years experience on the route. I am informed that Mr. Wood is prepared to carry on the service at $960 per annum.
It would be appreciated if the necessary action could be taken to have Mr. Wood maintain the service at this price.
Yours very truly,
Robbins L. Elliott,
Private Secretary.
Mr. Smith was then notified that the department would not proceed with the signing of the contract. I am supposed to believe that there was no political interference. I know that the officials of the Post Office Department were just as incensed as Mr. Smith and I. I tell the minister now

that if there is to be political jobbery carried on under this bill, which we of the opposition are now supporting, we will hold him responsible. He and his department will not be keeping faith with us, with the staff or with the public with respect to the passing of this bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTRACTS FOR CONVEYING MAIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few remarks on the bill before it receives third reading. Last Friday night, March 27, the bill received second reading and was considered in committee. At that time the chairman of the committee of the whole pointed out that the bill had been carefully considered by a special committee appointed to consider it and had been reported to the house without amendment. However, considerable discussion took place, and it seemed that nobody in the committee that evening could find any report that had been made by the special committee that had been established to deal with this most important matter.
I want to say at the very beginning that I am not opposed to the bill except for one reason. There seemed to be a great hurry to get it passed the other night, and in my dealings with the Post Office Department, especially with respect to the building of post offices, I have never found them in a hurry in my life. It took seven years of talking before they showed any signs of taking action, and I could not understand why they wanted to rush this measure through so rapidly the other night. As a matter of fact, under the rules of the house it should not have been reported from the committee. At ten o'clock we were still discussing the bill, and the committee should have risen, reported progress and asked leave to sit again. In spite of the fact that a great number of members objected to what was being done, the bill was reported from the committee and it is now before the house for third reading. I think that is contrary to the rules of the house.
I believe the bill should still stand over until the special committee has had another meeting or two. We looked to this committee to deal with the problems of the rural mail couriers throughout Canada, but after the bill has received third reading they will not have the authority to do so any more and the whole matter will be whitewashed. I doubt if they will have any more meetings. Looking at the reports of the proceedings of the two or three meetings they did hold- I think there have been two printed so far- there is nothing in them except the statements of the Postmaster General and his
Post Office Act
deputy. As I have said before, this legislation simply gives them more power. It does not take any power from them but adds to their powers so that they can be almost as dictatorial as they wish to be. We are back in the old days of patronage so far as the letting of contracts is concerned.
The special committee should make recommendations before the bill passes. They were appointed for the purpose of making recommendations with respect to the mail couriers and their problems. We even find that no representatives of the mail couriers were heard. That should not be. I think at least some of the mail couriers have a right to be called before the committee and heard, and if they were in any other walk of life they would be. If it should be decided that it is not necessary to hear them, then there are members on the committee representing every province in Canada and they should bring forward recommendations on behalf of the mail couriers in their provinces.
I have discussed the question of the rural mail couriers year after year when the post office estimates have been before us. We have no opportunity to discuss the pros and cons of this bill which is being pushed through so rapidly and we are no better off than we were. The only opportunity we will have will be when the estimates of the department are being considered, and we will have to spend a great deal of time then to get the information we desire. I have referred many times to the great discrimination that exists in the letting of contracts to mail couriers. I cited two or three instances recently and I should like to cite a couple now.
I have in mind a mail courier whose contract ends in 1955 and another one whose contract ends in 1956. The man whose contract ends in 1955 has to drive a distance of 61 miles. In the summer he can use a car. In the fall, winter and spring he must use a horse and cutter or horse and wagon. All these factors should have a bearing on what he is paid under his contract. As I said a moment ago, he has to drive 61 miles every day to complete his route. For that distance he gets the princely sum of $1,440 a year, a very small wage even if it were all profit. It takes him most of the day to complete the route. We all know that if he uses a car it will take at least three gallons of gas. He has 136 stops where he has boxes to attend to, and that means that he must use more gas. Taking into account the gas and oil that he uses, and without allowing anything for repairs to his car, we find that it

Post Office Act
would cost him $1.65 tor that one item which, taken from his $4.80, leaves him with a very small wage for himself, to say nothing of other expenses he might have.
We find that the man driving only 31 miles compared with the other man's 61 received $125 more. If that is not discrimination, then I do not know what discrimination is. That has been going on, and the Post Office Department now says that it wants more authority so that it can remedy such situations. If they were going to be able to remedy them under the bill, then I would vote for it a dozen times if I had a dozen votes. But they are only taking more authority into their hands without giving any assurance. The only assurance I know of was that mentioned the other night in the committee by the Postmaster General. When he was being questioned about the bill he said, as found at page 3387 of Hansard for March 27:
We always look at all the angles.
I suppose "we" means his associates in the Post Office Department.
Public interest was mentioned. That is one way of expressing what we are looking for. We want to see that the taxpayers of this country receive good service . . .
I can stop right there and say that there is no arm of the service, nothing in federal appointments and federal work done, to compare with the rural mail couriers who are doing an almost perfect job of work. I do not believe that there is a member in this house who will have very much complaint to the effect that people are not getting a thorough service from the mail couriers.
The Postmaster General goes on and says:
-and we want the man who is giving the service to be paid adequately.
I agree with that.
To achieve that we are looking at the security, the solvency of the men and the equipment, and a comparison of the routes, the number of boxes, the length of the routes: and all these considerations will be looked into and taken into consideration in the decision we are going to make.
Well, there is a recommendation that should come from the special committee, but they have not brought in any report as yet- any more than the evidence that was laid before them. They have made no recommendations.
When this bill passes, Mr. Speaker, the special committee will have no more power because the bill is already recorded as passed. I think that some action should be taken and that this should be passed over for a week or so. There is no great rush at the present time; they are not going to solve all of these cases; so let this committee bring in some recommendations that will be of benefit.

Again, I want to say that I am in favour of anything that will give more security and more wages to the mail couriers. Many of them today are not making 25 cents an hour. Yesterday I received a letter from one man who drives 56 miles. At this time of year it takes him 9| hours to complete that 56 miles, as he cannot use a car. He stated that he had to turn out the other morning at seven o'clock to start his route and he did not get through until half-past five. Of course, he might have had a half hour rest while getting his dinner somewhere on the route. However, when that man adds up what it costs him to feed his horse during the day I do not think he would be receiving any more than 15 cents or perhaps 16 cents an hour for the 9J hours he put in.
This is a most serious matter and yet we are rushing this bill through as though it were just another bill passing. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that this bill should be given further consideration, not only in the special committee but also in the committee of the house.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTRACTS FOR CONVEYING MAIL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a word in this connection as a member of that committee. I think that the hon. member for Queens (Mr. McLure) has either been misinformed or possibly does not understand-and that is the kindest way I can put it. It is the first time since I have been in the house that it has been said that no member of a committee knew what they were doing. I want to point out, Mr. Speaker, that it may be all very well for home consumption in Hansard, but the previous speaker never made one suggestion as to how we could improve conditions for the rural mail couriers. He suggests that the special committee did not consider the matter; but I want to assure him, as a member of that committee, that we did consider it. We asked for suggestions as to how we could best improve the plight of the rural mail couriers. We did not have any better suggestions. We do not say and have never said that this bill is perfect. We knew of nothing better to bring in at this time to assist the mail courier-the very man whom he has read about today-and he must be an exceptional man to drive 56 miles in the snow with a horse in one day. That man is a very good man and certainly he must have an imported horse to do it.

speechtext:
No, we do not have any horses like that, and we do not abuse any kind of animal. It is wrong to say that the committee did not endeavour to do anything. The member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), a very

superior member in any party, let alone where he sits, realized that we were trying to do something. The opposition had as good members on that committee as there were from other parties. They were just as sincere as any members of the committee and they would have liked to bring down something that would have solved the problem. However, they also realized, as the hon. member for Queens apparently does not, that conditions vary in each riding within a province, and that in each province of Canada climatic and other conditions also vary.
I would like the hon. member for Queens to take an hour and a half or five hours of the time of this house-well, not of this house because we have business to do-and come up to my office or, if he likes, up to the committee room, and make one concrete suggestion about how he would solve this problem in all provinces of Canada.
The new bill, I think, is discretionary and it is an endeavour to assist the very men he has been mentioning who are underpaid but who work on a voluntary bid. Nobody told them to bid the rate they did on their particular contracts. They had a right to bid as they saw fit and possibly they bid too low. The minister now has at least discretionary powers to assist in that particular route and in other routes. So, Mr. Speaker, I very much resent the insinuation that this committee, composed of members of all parties, did nothing. They made a sincere effort and we discussed the matter among ourselves. If the hon. member for Queens will read the evidence he will see where we asked whether anyone had anything better to offer in the interests of the rural mail couriers. We received nothing more concrete. We considered, as I am sure the hon. member has too, the possibility of establishing a mileage basis, or a set salary and a gasoline allowance, as well as whether these should be civil service appointments. In our judgment we know of no better system at the present time to assist the couriers-and above all to assist the man to whom he has just referred-not next year, not ten years from now, but as soon as this bill is passed.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONTRACTS FOR CONVEYING MAIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I should make a few comments on this at this time as I was a member of the committee. Bill 107, which was presented to amend the Post Office Act, was a very simple bill. Two years ago a bill was introduced to amend the Post Office Act which gave the postal authorities jurisdiction or authority to adjust salaries where necessary on any contract up to $1,000 but not beyond that. To me that was quite an unfair piece of legislation. If it was fair to
Post Office Act
adjust salaries up to $1,000 it should also have applied to contracts for $1,100 or $1,200 or any other amount. This bill merely extends the legislation of 1951, to embrace a contract of any size so that the authorities after inquiry may make adjustments.
I can quite readily see that it was not very fair to try to renew contracts on the same basis as applied four years ago because the couriers have a lot more work to do in suburban areas. They have literally hundreds more of boxes. If I understand the bill, and if I understand the Postmaster General, each case will be gone into individually and adjustments will be made or will be provided for to take care of any situation in any rural route regardless of where it may be situated.
I believe that this amending bill is at least a step in the right direction and that it was pretty well considered. The member for Queens, who has just spoken, has said that there were no recommendations. However, at the time we probably could have made some recommendations but they would not affect this bill. The post office committee will make suggestions to the government and I hope that they will be unanimous in an effort to put this whole policy on a much higher level than it is today.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is an appropriate time to discuss a subject that has been

mentioned on different occasions in this house before. Now, however, is the opportunity to relate the discussion directly to the proposal that is before us.
In this legislation we are dealing with an amendment to the Excise Tax Act which makes changes in our general excise taxation structure. Hence, this is an appropriate occasion on which to consider suggestions that should be made in connection with changes of that kind. The proposal before us represents the suggestions which the government now wishes to make. I wish to discuss another matter which I believe should be dealt with. I think this is the appropriate time to raise it. By presenting it at this time the opportunity is then afforded the government to see the proposal and to indicate its willingness or otherwise to accept the suggestion which has been made.
From the municipalities throughout the whole of Canada there has been an increasing demand that consideration be given to the fact that they are called upon to pay excise taxes including the 10 per cent sales tax on those things they buy for their own service of the people in their own communities. This applies also to purchases made by boards of education for the equipment that goes into the schools where education is given to the children of this country. It does seem to be an anomaly that the dominion government should recognize the fact that it is not appropriate to apply the excise taxes including the 10 per cent sales tax in the case of purchases made by provincial governments but that it should insist that municipal councils and school boards pay those taxes. The thing even goes further than the payment of taxes in the ordinary way. If municipalities within their own boundaries manufacture goods for their own requirements, these taxes still apply, although the goods are going to be used within the very municipal boundaries within which they have been made.
This is a matter of great importance at this time. Certain steps that have been taken by this government have imposed still heavier burdens upon the municipalities. This is not the occasion to argue the wisdom or otherwise of the course which has been followed. It should be pointed out, however, that there are in Canada many people who believe that civil defence is part of the general defence requirements of Canada. If that is so, then it does seem doubly onerous that those municipalities which are called upon to purchase special equipment for civil defence should find themselves not only bound to buy equipment which they do not think they should pay for in the first place, but on top of that they are called upon to pay sales tax and

other excise taxes to the senior government which imposes that necessity upon them.
This aggravates a situation which already is a source of great concern to many municipalities. Some municipalities, situated in what are obviously danger zones, have heavier obligations in this respect than have municipalities which would not be likely targets of air attack. Therefore they not only are called upon to meet a feature of defence which is part of our general problem of national defence, but are called upon to pay excise taxes including sales tax on the equipment they must buy as well.
This subject has been further aggravated in many communities by the fact that, with the extension of the acquisition of land for various purposes by the government of Canada, more and more land is exempted from taxation within some communities, a fact which throws a still greater burden back upon those municipal taxpayers who in turn must pay those special taxes imposed by the dominion government.
There are many anomalies in connection with this situation. Let us think of some of the highways that go through various provinces. Those highways may follow a route which carries them through large urban municipalities. Up to the boundary of that municipality the road-building equipment or road-repairing equipment acquired by the provincial government pays none of the special excise taxes including sales tax, but the municipality supporting the continuation of that highway through the urban area, with its own equipment, is called upon to pay these excise taxes upon that equipment serving exactly the same purpose up to the two boundary lines of the municipality. Surely that is utterly inconsistent with the fact that in this case the provincial government and the municipal governments-which is what the municipal councils in fact really are-are performing similar duties on behalf of those taxpayers whom they serve. Surely if it is appropriate that this exemption apply to provincial authorities performing the same task, the exemption should apply to those who continue that responsibility through the intervening segment of the same undertaking.
This illustration could be carried forward into a great many other activities but I shall leave it there because it seems to me that the illustration X have offered does indicate the anomaly that presents itself.
The municipalities of Canada for a number of years have been emphasizing their difficulties in this respect, and X think I should place on record the resolution which was adopted by the mayors association and which was presented to the government of Canada. It
Excise Tax Act
deals directly with this point. It reads as follows:
Whereas municipalities are required to pay the federal 10 per cent sales tax on all items purchased as well as on equipment and articles manufactured by municipalities for their own use and not for resale; and
Whereas the provincial governments, their boards and commissions, do not pay the federal sales tax nor is the tax exigible on certain items purchased for use by hospitals and electrical utilities; and
Whereas municipal governments, under the British North America Act, derive their being from the provincial governments and, as such, represent the delegated power of provincial governments; and
Whereas therefore the continued imposition of the federal sales tax on the purchases of and equipment produced by municipalities would appear to be discriminatory; and
Whereas municipal governments are hard-pressed to hold the rising costs of local government within the narrow limits of their sources of revenue, a situation over which the federal government has expressed its solicitous concern; and
Whereas municipal governments, while desirous of co-operating fully with the organization and provision of adequate local civil defence, are nevertheless finding that the local costs of civil defence are adding an additional and onerous burden on their already severely restricted revenues:
Therefore be it resolved that the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities strongly urge the federal government to exempt the municipal governments from payment of the federal sales tax on all municipal purchases; including articles manufactured by municipalities for their own use and not for resale.
I submit that this resolution should commend itself to the government and that this is the appropriate time to draw to the attention of the government the fact that an amendment should be included in this present bill now before us which would meet this most reasonable request made by the representatives of many municipalities throughout Canada. In very moderate and conciliatory language this resolution points out that the rising costs of municipalities necessitate taxation within the narrow limits of municipal sources of revenue, which limits are more seriously curtailed by the extent of the tax dollar which is being taken from the Canadian taxpayer by the Canadian government at this time. It is all very well to say that the municipalities still have their flexible sources of revenue. They have only the sources of revenue which are left open to them after the dollars have been drained off in very large measure by the government of Canada.
If the taxpayers in these municipalities- after all, the taxpayers in the municipalities of Canada are the same taxpayers who pay provincial taxes as well as taxes to this government-were freed from the heavy burdens that are imposed by the central taxing authorities, they would be in a much better position to contribute to local requirements. Therefore the extent to which taxation by

Excise Tax Act
the central government constantly encroaches upon the tax dollar is a matter of real and direct concern to the municipal authorities responsible for local taxation.
We have seen the percentage of the tax dollar go up day by day until it appears that last year 78 cents out of every tax dollar was absorbed by this government, leaving only 22 cents available for both the provincial and the municipal authorities. Within that limit the municipalities must seek their opportunity to obtain the money that is required for the vitally important duties which they must carry on on behalf of the people living in those communities.
If we will only think for a moment of the duties performed by the municipal authorities it will become apparent that in the daily lives of our people it is those duties which are most directly related to the needs of our people. Water supply, light, sewage, roads, other services including fire and police protection; all these things are provided by the local governments. It is to the local government that the Canadian in most oases looks for the security and comfort and amenities of his daily life. Therefore, we must recognize the vital necessity of giving to these municipal authorities an adequate measure of independent authority over their own affairs which will assure the most effective services within this country of ours.
When we talk about building up Canadian society, let us remember the extent to which this society of ours rests upon the municipal structure.
Including education.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That of course is most important of all in the field of education. The whole character of our people in the years ahead, the whole future of our country as a civilized society, is going to depend upon the kind of education that we give our children. In very large measure today the burden imposed upon the municipal taxpayer for taxation is seriously aggravated by these excise and sales taxes which are incorporated in the purchases made necessary by the expanding needs of education. Surely if there is one place where exemption in regard to excise and sales tax should apply, it is in the educational requirements upon which to a very great degree the whole future of our society is going to rest.
There is no miracle by which we can carry out the duties of government in the provinces or in the municipalities without taxation. Nevertheless there must be some places where the justice of the application of taxes must be given full consideration. I recognize that

there is a difference between the status of provincial governments, municipal councils and the school boards; nevertheless when we speak of the municipalities as creatures of the provinces I would recall the fact that they are fairly lusty and vigorous creatures. They are not creatures to be disposed of by the whim of any government, either the government in Ottawa or any provincial government responsible for the administration of municipal laws within the province. These are real and vital communities within our combined social structure.
I do suggest therefore, as has been pointed out by the federation of mayors and municipalities, that since municipal councils and school boards exist under laws passed by the provincial legislatures, and are to that extent local emanations of the provincial legislative bodies, it would be consistent to apply to those municipal authorities the same exemptions as are applied to the provincial governments.
I would point out that there might be created an invitation to follow a course which might present some difficulty. I would think that if taxes of this kind are to be continued there will be another invitation to centralize authority. After all, one way in which the municipalities could be relieved from this would be for them to turn over certain of their responsibilities to the provincial governments in return for payment and then the provincial governments could buy this machinery and equipment without paying any excise or sales taxes. Thus you would have centralization into provincial hands and still further centralization into the hands of the government at Ottawa. I realize that that appeals to the centralist party from which this government is formed. It believes in centralization for the sake of centralization.

A number of speakers in the course of the budget debate raised this question, as I think they did on the budget resolutions as well.
As I said a moment ago, and perhaps my hon. friend will forgive me if I say it now, he has thrown no new light on this very important and difficult question. I do not feel I can recommend the exemption that was asked for and I would like now to give to the house the reasons for taking the position which I have-a position which, I may say, I found it necessary to take in previous years.
In the first place, I want to assure the various municipal officials that I am not lacking in sympathy for the problems which they face in raising the necessary moneys to finance local government services. It is not a pleasant business to tax people to find moneys to provide things they want and are asking for, as I have every reason to know, since I have to do it myself. However, I am sure that these municipal officials will realize that I must be something less than enthusiastic if by relieving their burdens I add to my own problems. The municipalities, to use the words of my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition, are legal emanations of the provinces. As I said to the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) the other day, I think it would be highly inappropriate for the federal government to assume any direct responsibility for the financial problems of municipalities. Clearly the federal government should follow the line which it has been following of dealing directly with the provincial governments themselves in financial matters, rather than attempting to assist municipalities directly by tax relief measures.
Now, as to the matter of sales tax on materials purchased by the municipalities, and coming down to the first principle, if articles are subject to sales tax in the hands of individuals I find it a little difficult to see why they should be exempt from tax if they are purchased by a corporation for use by individuals. I think it is reasonable to say that perhaps in their very understandable

request for tax relief in this appeal the municipalities have not a great deal of logic on their side. It is true that the provinces are exempt from sales tax on articles purchased by them for provincial use; and a similar provision, I understand, applies to provincial boards. But, in addition to the substantial losses of revenue, which would be involved if municipal purchases were exempt from sales tax, and which would have to be made up from somewhere else, there is a very real practical problem involved in complying with this request. As the house is aware, the sales tax is put on at the manufacturer's level and the ordinary manufacturer has no way of knowing who the eventual purchaser of his product is going to be-whether it will be a municipality or an individual businessman. Accordingly, if an exemption of this kind were granted it would be necessary to fall back on the device of taking either a certificate as to use or the adoption of a system of refunding. Either method is fairly cumbersome and involves a great deal of paper work. When we stop to realize that there are over 4,000 municipalities in Canada, and that the range of articles that can be purchased is an extremely wide range, I do not think I need to emphasize the difficulties of attempting to administer any such exemption. In saying that, I feel sure it will be appreciated that I am not in any way reflecting on the integrity and good will of the municipal officials.
Taking all of these factors into consideration, I have come to the conclusion this year, as I have in past years, that an exemption of this kind cannot and should not be recommended. That is the reason why it is not contained in the amendment before the house.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while not agreeing with all of the arguments which the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) put forth in support of this proposition, I wish to say that we thoroughly agree with the contention put forward by the federation of mayors and municipalities, that municipalities be exempted from the requirement to pay excise or sales tax on their purchases.
I have listened to the defence just made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) for his failure to accede to this request and I must say that I, for one, am not convinced that he has made any case for his failure to recommend this change.
Not only have we had the position stated by the Minister of Finance here today, and on other occasions, but he has also favoured some of us with excerpts from letters which he has written to some of the cities and municipalities which have made representations to him. I have in my hand a copy of 68108-220
Excise Tax Act
a letter which the Minister of Finance wrote to me on March 18 of this year in reply to my representations in support of a resolution on this matter submitted to the government by the council of the city of Winnipeg. In this letter to me the Minister of Finance has given me excerpts from the letter which he wrote to Mr. Gardner, the Winnipeg city clerk; and one of these arguments which has already been given us but which is spelled out here seems to me to be quite unconvincing. I am quoting from the minister's own letter to the city of Winnipeg.
An exemption from sales tax for materials and supplies purchased by municipal governments would result in lower costs to the municipalities and therefore should bring some net reduction in municipal taxes but municipal taxpayers are usually also federal taxpayers as well, and tax savings gained at the municipal level might have to be given up in their payment of federal taxes.
It is that point to which I should like to make answer. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), and indeed others who have spoken on this matter thus far in today's debate, seem to ignore the fact that municipal taxation is levied on a different basis from that of federal taxation. There is a good deal that is wrong with the basis of federal taxation, but at least it comes nearer to the ability to pay basis than any other jurisdiction in this country is able to come. If this policy did work out as the Minister of Finance suggests, that there would be a slight reduction in cost to citizens as municipal taxpayers which they would have to make up in their capacity as federal taxpayers, I suggest that is all to the good. It would mean that that difference would be transferred from a basis which is predicated upon ownership of real estate to an ability to pay basis, at least in so far as that principle is involved in federal taxation. I submit therefore, Mr. Speaker, that the main argument in terms of principle that the Minister of Finance has used in his letter to the city of Winnipeg really does not hold water.
Of course, it is the same people who must pay taxes, whether they pay them to municipalities, provinces or to the federal government. Our whole concern in respect to the question of taxation is that it should be put, as nearly as possible, on an ability to pay basis. The two forms of taxation which come closest to that are the personal income tax and the corporation income tax. We feel, therefore, that it would be better that municipal taxpayers as such should enjoy some relief from municipalities not having to pay the sales tax, even if they do have to turn around and make up for that by paying it in federal taxation.

Excise Tax Act
Now, Mr. Speaker, the other argument which the Minister of Finance used today, and he used it in this letter which he wrote to the Winnipeg city clerk to which I have already referred, is the question of administration. Again I must confess that we are not convinced that that is an insurmountable obstacle. After all, the minister admits that the administration of this tax is already a complicated procedure, with many exemptions as to commodities and many exemptions as to purchasers already involved in the legislation. I, for one, cannot see how it is possible to draw a line between provincial governments and hospitals on the one hand, and municipalities and school boards on the other. I feel that the federation of mayors and municipalities is quite correct in pressing the government for an exemption from the payment of the sales tax.
Actually of course, Mr. Speaker, this raises the whole question as to the fairness of the sales tax. If it is unfair, as we are contending, to impose it upon municipal taxpayers in their capacity as municipal taxpayers, we take that position because we feel that it is unfair to impose it upon them as individuals. Our opposition to the sales tax goes much further than just our opposition to municipalities being required to pay it. We oppose the sales tax in principle. We realize that a great many attempts have been made, particularly in recent years in this house and in some of the committees that have dealt with this matter, to build up the sales tax as a socially desirable method of obtaining revenue. In my opinion it is still a bad form of taxation.
In the course of this session we have heard a great deal said about secret orders in council-at least about one secret order in council which is in existence in this country today. I do not like secret orders in council, not even one of them. But I submit, Mr. Speaker, that hidden taxation is even more sinister and more harmful to the average Canadian than is a secret order in council. That is what we have in the sales tax. Maybe you cannot call it a secret tax because it is there on the books. Anyone who wants to read about it can learn about it. However, it is a hidden form of taxation. It hits all of those people who are not in income brackets sufficiently high to be paying personal income taxes. As a matter of fact, I feel that the Minister of Finance admitted that the sales tax is that kind of hidden tax that gets at everybody, whether or not they have sufficient income, in this same letter from which I have already quoted and which

he wrote to Mr. Gardner, the city clerk in Winnipeg. He said this:
It is naturally the desire of the federal government to keep the sales tax base as broad as possible.
He was stating that as an argument for imposing these taxes on municipalities and school boards. I suggest he has let the cat out of the bag. What he likes about the sales tax is that he catches all those poor people to whom he is giving the impression, by his income tax exemption levels, that they are not being taxed. The plain fact of the matter is that every single man who has an income of less than $1,000, every married man whose income is less than $2,000, and every married man with two children whose income is less than $2,300, though he may not be paying the personal income tax, is certainly caught in the taxation net through this hidden tax which we know as the sales tax. We agree, therefore, with the stand taken by the federation of mayors and municipalities. We agree with the stand taken by the city council of my home city of Winnipeg, that municipalities and school boards should be exempted from paying this tax. We go much further and say that the whole basis of taxation should be pulled away from this taxation on the basis of what one has to purchase and moved in the direction of taxation on the basis of ability to pay.
I give the government little credit-very little; that is all they are entitled to-for moving a little bit in that direction. In looking at the figures which were given to us on February 19, we discovered that the total revenue from excise taxes in the year ended March 31, 1952 amounted to 22 per cent of the total revenue of the federal government. In the year ended March 31, 1952 the estimate was that excise taxes would account for only 19'5 per cent of the total revenue; that, of course, is just one form of indirect taxation. If you add all the forms of indirect taxation together, you find that they accounted for 36-6 per cent in the fiscal year 1952 and 34-3 per cent in the fiscal year ended March 31, 1953. As I say, I am prepared to give the government what little credit is coming to it for having adjusted things so that that percentage is shifting slightly. But our contention is that for 34-3 per cent of the government's revenue still to be coming from what I will call secret or hidden taxes, is unfair to those in the lower income brackets, those little people whom the Minister of Finance would have us believe are not paying income taxes but who are caught in this legislation. This Excise Tax Act is indeed, Mr. Speaker, an income tax act for the little fellow with very little income.

Mr. Speaker, I am not at all sure that I can throw any more light on the question than has already been thrown on it, but I do feel that those of us who have been speaking in this house for quite a number of years on the sales tax, and advocating its removal, showing thereby that we are opposed to the sales tax in principle, ought to indicate our support of the principle of the amendment which was introduced by the Leader of the Opposition this afternoon and say something by way of reply to the reasons which were given by the Minister of Finance for the position he has taken in respect to this appeal by the federation of mayors and municipalities.
At the outset I want to indicate my support of the brief that was presented by the federation of mayors and municipalities to the Minister of Finance. Contrary to what the Minister of Finance said, I think there was much logic in their position and in their case. The Minister of Finance said there was not. I hope I shall be able to show that there was at least a little logic, perhaps as much as the Minister of Finance has shown in the position that he has taken.
For a good many years I have been working with a view to getting this job done, and lending what little help I could to Anally convince the Minister of Finance that he should grant exemption from sales tax to the municipalities and school boards across Canada on the equipment that had been purchased by them. They are entitled to it. They have been asking for it for a good many years, and they have been showing excellent reasons why the Minister of Finance should grant it.
Having said that, I should like to turn for just a moment to some of the things the Minister of Finance said in his statement this afternoon. He said he was not lacking in sympathy for the case of the municipalities. Perhaps not, but the municipalities in the country are likely to judge more by deeds than by words in a case of this kind.

Not only the municipalities, of course, but also a very large number of individuals who are directly or indirectly affected by the position taken by the minister. He says that it is a mistake for the federal government to assume any direct responsibility for the municipalities that are legal emanations of the provinces. I admit that the municipalities are legal emanations; they are the children of the provincial governments. That is quite true. But there would be considerably more logic in what the minister said if the federal government had not already laid

down a precedent. I am going to mention only one; there are probably many that could be mentioned.
A number of years ago, during the depression years, the municipalities of Canada were in a bad position financially as a consequence of extremely low prices for farm products and the heavy burden of relief costs. The federal government was induced at that time to put through this very house a bill called the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act by which the then minister of finance was able to extend directly to the municipalities loans at a rate of interest of 2 per cent on self-liquidating projects. The provincial governments were drawn into it indirectly to give what they called a continuing guarantee, but the assistance was granted directly to the municipalities.
I therefore contend that the government thereby laid down a precedent for taking other action that might be considered as direct assistance to the municipalities. The minister therefore cannot just shrug it off like that and say, "It is none of our affair" because these are the legal children of the provincial governments. I do not think his reason in that respect holds any water.
The second thing he said was that if he granted the request by the federation of mayors and municipalities his department would lose a substantial amount of revenue. I think that is perhaps the best reason he gave today, namely that he would lose some substantial revenue. But, Mr. Speaker, if the Minister of Finance should comply with the request of the municipalities, school districts and others in the country for the removal of the sales tax on equipment they have to purchase, he could make up that revenue in some other way and, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has so well said, in a way that would be more fair and equitable. Certainly the principle of taxation according to ability to pay is much to be preferred to taxation where you can grab it easiest. The principle that seems to be followed today is to get the taxes just as easily as you can and to make others the collectors of taxes, not go out and do it yourself; make other people do it for you.
I suggest there is much reason in what my friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said. Certainly an income tax or some such thing based on ability to pay is to be preferred to a tax like the sales tax which does have the effect of pyramiding consumer prices, a situation which throws an unjustifiable burden upon those people least able to bear it. I have always opposed the sales tax in principle for the reason that it was applied

at the manufacturer's level and had the effect of pyramiding prices; and in this house on a good many occasions I have given my reasons for being opposed to it in principle.
The Minister of Finance said there was a practical difficulty in the way of granting the request of the federation of mayors and municipalities. He said that the excise tax is imposed at the manufacturer's level and that therefore to comply with their request would involve a system of refunds and a good deal of paper work. I think perhaps that is true, Mr. Speaker; I must say that in all fairness to the minister. I can quite well visualize what a complication of paper work would be involved in trying to deal with purchases made by 4,000 different municipal governments in this country if the exemption were to be granted on all their purchases. I can quite well understand that, because it would perhaps involve everything from mops, mop sticks, soap and things of that kind up to machinery that costs a great deal of money.
Horses?

I do not know whether they use horses out in the municipalities or not, but I think we have already said too much about horses. Let us therefore leave them out for the time being. If there is a practical difficulty, however, I suggest that nobody created that difficulty but the government itself that devised the kind of tax that is imposed at the manufacturer's level and that would require the kind of complicated paper work the minister suggested would be involved if exemptions were to be granted.
But let me just make this suggestion to him. If he would make a start now and grant the exemptions requested by the mayors and municipalities and school boards on heavy machinery and equipment that is required for their road-building programs; on equipment, costing a good deal of money, used for the purpose of conveying children to school, such as vans and that sort of thing; and on that costly equipment that is used in civil defence -if the minister would begin by exempting those items only I think he would find that the paper work would not be too extensive.
Certainly the government does not shrink today from exemptions to various sections of Canadian society such as the farmers, with respect to customs duty and such things as that on equipment used exclusively in farming. That process of exemption does involve making refunds. The refunds have to be applied for. Paper work is necessary. While it is perfectly true, Mr. Speaker, that it becomes complicated and in many instances the applicant for the refund has to wait many weeks or months for his money-and that fact has been drawn to the attention of
Excise Tax Act
the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) on several occasions during these past few weeks-in spite of those things I feel perfectly satisfied that if the Minister of Finance would now begin to accede to the request of the federation of mayors and municipalities by granting exemption from sales tax on heavy equipment that is essential for civil defence and for the transport of children to schools, he would be showing his good faith and perhaps would be taking a step toward eventual complete exemption that might be arranged, with little complication, later on.
I just want to conclude by saying this. I do not think for one moment that there is any good and sound reason why the Minister of Finance could not at least begin to take the action that has been requested by the mayors and municipalities. May I say this. I think he owes it to the municipalities of Canada to help them in these extremely trying times. The municipalities are carrying terrific loads. Many of them are growing rapidly. They are bursting at the seams. In their efforts to look after the people who are coming into the municipalities as Canada grows and expands, they are hard put to it to find the revenues with which to provide the extension of services. The unusual demands for education place another burden upon the municipalities and upon the taxpayers in those municipalities.
When one considers that many municipalities in this country are servicing federal property and are not receiving one cent of taxes from the federal government for so doing, unless they come in the class that has been provided for in this municipal arrangement that takes into consideration, I think, only the larger cities where there is a concentration of government offices and buildings, and government property, I think under those circumstances one could very truthfully say that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) owes it to the municipalities of the country to grant their request. I want it known that I support the brief that was sent in by the federation of mayors and municipalities.
As to the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), whether it is found to be out of order or in order I want to say now that I will support it if it comes to a vote.

The over-all cost to Canada's economy could amount to hundreds of millions of dollars. I believe the price is far too high to allow nationalist emotions to override common sense. Since last May, when I outlined to the house a proposed national gas policy, there have been some important developments. Planning for gas markets on a larger scale than before is now required because of the continuing rapid expansion of proved gas reserves in the west and also because of the increasing wastage of gas in the Alberta oil fields where gas must be produced whether or not it has a market.
In other words, we have entered an era of gas plenty rather than shortage that will likely continue for many years provided the incentive is continued for large-scale exploration. Maximum value with minimum waste can only be achieved in my opinion by pipeline route planning designed to capture maximum markets on both sides of the border on a sound basis with the least possible delay. To do so we must carefully consider more than the three alternative pipe-line projects east that were before us last year. Let me emphasize that I am neither supporting nor opposing any particular would-be builder of

Mid-Continent Pipelines Limited a pipe line. I am not concerned with what one of several pipe-line proposers, or what combination of proposers, actually builds what I trust will be only the first of several major pipe lines eastward from Alberta.
I am very much concerned, however, with the selection of a route because that decision will be vital in its long-term effect upon the west and upon all of Canada. The mating of gas reserves to markets should be, as has largely been the case with our crude oil, on the soundest possible economic basis, meaning simply to ensure the best possible price for gas producers and the lowest possible cost to gas consumers. Let me emphasize that our gas, like our oil, is a long cost-distance removed from the major markets beyond the prairies. Even with the most economic mating of reserves to markets, our wellhead worth of gas and oil is and will continue to be substantially lower than the wellhead value of the same quality products in major United States producing states, which are better located in relation to major markets.
Despite that handicap we can continue to attract hundreds of millions of exploration dollars, which are essential if the underground treasures of the west are to be fully uncovered. We can reduce the handicap of long cost-distance by keeping the economic climate healthy. Part of that climate involves, in my view, the application of sound economics and common sense, not emotionalism and nationalism, to the linking of reserves to markets. In the routing of the Interprovincial oil pipe line from Alberta to the east, sound economics won out over what I believe to be the emotional appeal of construction confined solely to Canadian territory. With further savings in oil transport costs to be achieved in a few months by the extension of the pipe line 600 odd miles from Superior to Sarnia, the wellhead worth of western Canadian oil will be further increased a few cents to about 15 cents per barrel above the price that would apply if an all-Canadian route had been followed.
That represents, on our current proved oil reserves alone, about a $300 million saving for the Canadian economy. The Canadian government through corporation taxes, and the governments of oil provinces through royalties, will collect over half that increased value as the oil is produced. Indeed, they and Canada will benefit even more, for the balance of the added value will go to those who risked capital in oil and gas development-

I would like to complete my comments in relation to the oil line because it has a very direct bearing on the particular pipe line before us. I mentioned that there would be a huge saving to the Canadian economy, about $300 million, because of the routing of this pipe line by way of the United States to Sarnia. I might say that big saving to Canada is not at the expense of the eastern Canadian consumer. The consumer in the east pays no more and no less than he would if his petroleum supply were from outside Canada, for Alberta oil must be laid down in Ontario refineries at no more than the laid-down price of United States oil. The western producer and his government partners get that competitive price less the transport cost; and the lower the transport cost-in other words the more economical the pipe line-the higher is the wellhead return.
The pricing of natural gas to the producer and consumer is also based upon competition not only from gas from other fields but also from the other principal fuels of home and industry, namely fuel oil and coal. In some markets, those close to gas fields like many Alberta communities, and others close to some pipe lines, the cost of gas is or may be lower than that of other fuels. In other markets such as the vast fuel market of eastern Canada our western gas at best can only approach or meet the cost of fuel oil or coal.
At worst, by which I mean through use of the most expensive rather than the lowest cost pipe-line route, western gas would not be able to meet competition of other fuels without one or more forms of assistance. First, there might be some major form of either direct or indirect subsidy paid by the Canadian consumers as a whole or by the

eastern consuming provinces. Second, there might have to be a substantial degree of equalizing of costs to consumers along the entire pipe-line route, designed to bring costs down in markets most distant from the gas fields, and raise costs in markets along the route. This would have the effect of prairie province consumers along the route being forced to help subsidize gas in eastern Canada. Third, there might be a cutting down of wellhead values for gas in the fields serving the pipe line, thus forcing the producer and all who share in the proceeds of his gas production to help subsidize gas for eastern Canada; or we might have a combination of the various forms of subsidy I have already mentioned.
Certainly the Minister of Trade and Commerce is not unaware of most of the points I have made in regard to oil and gas pricing and related matters.

He spoke on March 13 in this debate dealing with the Interprovincial pipe line, and referred to suggestions that the pipe line should have gone from Alberta to Port Arthur, and then around the north and east side of the great lakes to Sarnia, rather than enter the United States and thence cross Michigan to Sarnia. It is worth noting that the distance from Gretna. Manitoba, to Sarnia by the present route is 939 miles, while the distance by the route advocated ... is 1,341 miles.

The cost increase involved in building the pipe line following the latter route would result in an additional expenditure estimated at $67 million. Such a line would touch no important refining centre and thus would be of no important value to the area it would traverse. Remembering that the cost of the line must eventually be paid either by the producers or by the users of gasoline and other petroleum products, or by both, the government is not disposed to exercise its authority to saddle these consumers with an additional and unnecessary $67 million of expenditure, nor would the national interest be served by so doing.
In that basic conclusion I fully concur. It supports the case I have presented many times since the pipe line was first proposed in 1949. However, the minister is not quite correct on one point. The consumer of oil moved over the line would not have to pay the extra S67 million, for the cost to him has a ceiling set by competition with foreign oil. The extra cost would be recovered by a higher transport charge passed back to the producer, and would thus be a burden upon the oil producer,
