The minister showed his basic awareness of the economic weakness of a gas pipe line from Alberta to eastern Canada over the Canadian north-great lakes route when he commented unfavourably upon an oil pipe line over the same route. He also showed his realization of the economic unsoundness of this line or the weakness of the line when he wrote Premier Manning of Alberta concerning gas pipe lines last January 3. The minister quoted his letter during his speech on March 13. After advising the Alberta premier that before any export permit for gas to the United States would be authorized under the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act, Ontario, Quebec and prairie markets must have Alberta gas made available, the minister then went on to say:
I am aware that, for the period when natural gas is first made available in Ontario and Quebec, and until the load can be built up, such a pipeline project is unlikely to be profitable, either for the producers of gas or for the owners of the pipe line. Nevertheless, there is evidence that a pipeline project for Ontario and Quebec can be worked out and that the project will be profitable over a period of years.
During his speech the minister made reasonably clear the particular route about which he was thinking. On page 2930 of Hansard for March 13, 1953, the minister said:
I am convinced, after thorough study of the matter, that the only reliable supply of natural gas for the provinces of Ontario and Quebec must be from western Canada by means of an allCanadian pipe line.
I am glad to see that the minister has just entered the chamber. The minister's statements might be summarized as follows. An oil pipe line from Alberta to eastern Canada, by an all-Canadian route in preference to the route chosen, would be plain silly because it would be 400 miles longer and would cost $67 million extra. It would be an extra drain on the Canadian economy, and would serve no useful purpose. A gas pipe line over the same costly all-Canadian route would also lose money for the producers and in addition for the owners of the pipe line for some time-the number of years he did not indicate-but that is the only gas line my government will approve because that is the only reliable way of getting gas to eastern Canada. I am paraphrasing the statement by the minister.
Like my chief, the Leader of the Opposition, like the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and like all others who have spoken in this debate from all parties in this house, I strongly support putting the west's gas to
[Mr. Nickle.l

use for Canada and getting natural gas to as many Canadians as possible. I submit, however, that there are several alternatives to an Alberta to Quebec gas pipe line built entirely on Canadian soil, each of which would be more economically sound, would provide a better deal for Canadian producers and consumers as well as for the backers of the pipe line, and would better serve the interests of the gas provinces and Canada as a whole.
These alternatives are: (1) A gas exchange treaty with the United States; (2) a pipe line from Alberta to eastern Canada dedicated to serving only Canadian consumers and following one of the two shortest cost-distance routes. Such a line would cross the prairie provinces, serving this market, then parallel the Interprovincial oil pipe line along the south side of Lake Superior and then reenter Canada either at Sault Ste. Marie or near Sarnia; (3) a comparable route from Alberta to eastern Canada, with Canadian consumers having first priority on gas throughout, but with no barrier being placed on sales to United States consumers of gas available in excess of Canadian needs.
The first alternative would involve a sincere top-level effort by Canadian and United States governments to try to work out a long term, firm treaty for exchange of gas between the two countries. The purpose of such a treaty would be the matching of gas fields to gas markets in the two nations on the most economic basis; that is in a pattern designed to give producers in both countries the highest possible wellhead value, and consumers in both nations gas at lowest possible cost. Over the past year the leader of my party and others, including myself, have advocated that the government initiate negotiations with the United States to determine the feasibility of gas exchange. There is no evidence that any such negotiations have been initiated. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, in fact, confirmed this last May when he answered "no" to a direct question by me on the matter. He appears to further confirm it by his comment in this house on March 13, which appears at page 2930 of Hansard:
I am convinced that the rulings of the federal power commission which recognize the great and growing demand for natural gas in the United States debar any possibility of such an exchange.
How can the minister, or anyone else, actually know that a common sense gas exchange treaty is impossible of achievement until a real effort to get one has been made? Certainly at present the restrictions as to outside delivery of Canadian gas under the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act, and the restrictions on United States gas under

the United States federal power commission, may prove more costly to producers and consumers in both countries than their replacement by an exchange treaty based on the most economic matching of gas fields to markets.
It is a fact that a number of Pacific northwest and middle western states in the United Slates could be supplied with lower cost gas from Canada than from the United States fields. This would at the same time ensure that British Columbia, which is too small a market to support a pipe line unless that line also serves the United States northwest, could be supplied with Canadian gas. It would ensure, too, that Canadian gas producers, and their government partners in the proceeds of production, could get the best possible return from this resource. It is also a fact that United States gas from Texas and Louisiana could be piped into Ontario and Quebec at a cost to Canadian consumers from 10 to 20 per cent lower than the cost of Alberta gas delivered by even the most economic route.
The doubts of the Minister of Trade and Commerce concerning gas exchange, and the fears of others both in this house and elsewhere in Canada that dependence upon a foreign source of gas would mean insecurity, both as to supply and price, are shared by the United States in the Pacific northwest and Washington. There is the fear that dependence on Canadian gas could mean insecurity of supply and price. Such fears might, in fact, result in rejection by the United States of the Westcoast Transmission Company's proposal for a gas line from the Peace river fields of northern Alberta and British Columbia down to Vancouver, Seattle, Portland and other communities. At this stage of the federal power commission hearings on the Westcoast application, and the alternative proposal for dedication of the Pacific northwest to gas from more distant [DOT] United States fields, the odds are probably no better than even money that Westcoast can win out.
If this government is strongly desirous of Peace river gas reaching the Pacific it will likely have to give-despite the restrictions of the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act-the federal power commission a guarantee that the act would not be used to cut off gas supply to the United States northwest for at least twenty times the duration *of the present one-year export permit, and further guarantee that gas costs would not be raised to prohibitive levels by application [DOT]of the act's power to impose an export tax of up to ten cents per thousand cubic feet. When and if the government presents that
Mid-Continent Pipelines Limited guarantee-without which British Columbia might not get a gas pipe line-this government might logically raise in Washington the broad question of a large scale gas exchange treaty.
If we cannot get an exchange of gas, our own self-interest dictates that we try to secure certain United States gas markets in order to ensure gas for our Pacific coast and economic outlets for certain of our gas reserves. Since this would be of obvious value to the United States, too, gas supply to specified United States markets could at least be used as a lever to secure (1) concessions on United States markets for such items as the Canadian petrochemicals, which will be a vast by-product of gas export from Alberta; and (2) United States guarantees of precedence for Canadian consumers on gas pipe lines passing over United States territory between Canadian fields and markets.
If exchange of gas is proved impossible, let us consider the alternative routes for a pipe line between Alberta and eastern Canada. But first there are certain misconceptions in the east and in this house as to what a gas pipe line might achieve. The first misconception is the view that Alberta gas would be cheap gas in the east. That is not so. Gas delivered at the Alberta end of a pipe line would likely cost in the range of seven to ten cents per thousand cubic feet. The eastern home owner served by the line would likely pay 15 to 20 times that wellhead cost. The eastern industrial consumer would likely have to pay 4 to 8 times the wellhead cost.
Of necessity I use a broad range of estimated costs, for these would vary with the *pipe-line route chosen; the nature of direct or indirect subsidies, if such should be provided, the degree of success in building up markets through the years in competition with other fuels, especially industrial markets which would be expected to absorb 70 per cent or more of the pipe line throughout. Every potential consumer, householder or industry, would have to make his own decision to use or not to use gas, based upon its cost in comparison to other fuels, the cost of changeover from one fuel to another, and the comparative convenience of fuels. By any pipe-line route, Alberta gas will not be cheap gas in the east; but it could be cheaper by one route in preference to another.
The second misconception in the east is the view that a pipe line would make gas available to all Ontario and Quebec. Actually a transport pipe line serves only the markets along its route; and supplies of gas to other towns or cities or industries 25, 50, 100 or several hundreds of miles distant

Mid-Continent Pipelines Limited from the main pipe line are dependent upon the economics of the particular branch or lateral lines that would have to be built to serve markets off the main line. For example, markets far larger than any now indicated would have to be available in northern Ontario to justify any branch lines from a main line north of lake Superior. Just as many smaller Alberta communities, some within 25 miles of gas fields or pipe lines, are too distant cost-wise to get natural gas, a far greater number of Ontario and Quebec communities cannot hope to be served with natural gas when a pipe line is built from the west.
The most costly section of a pipe line from Alberta to the east via Canadian territory would be the more than 800 miles in northern Ontario between the Manitoba border and the Sudbury area. The difficult terrain in that range would raise the mileage cost of construction by from 100 to 150 per cent above the cost of construction along the rest of the route. That 800-mile section would be a major contributing factor in making cost of a line over that route far higher than the cost of a line to eastern Canada via the United States. That big extra cost the producer, the consumer and the Canadian economy would have to pay.
What would be the benefit of an allCanadian pipe line north of the great lakes? The market survey made for Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited, the first proposer of a line over the all-Canadian route, anticipates that the total requirements of the communities to be served between Saskatchewan and Quebec inclusive would be 86 billion cubic feet the first year of pipe-line operation, building up to 105 billion the fifth year. Of that fifth year total, the survey indicates that only 4-6 billion cubic feet, or just 4-4 per cent of the total, would be the requirement along the costly 800-mile stretch including Port Arthur and Fort William and eight smaller communities between Manitoba and Sudbury which are the only markets contemplated to be served between Manitoba and Sudbury. The population represented is about 2 per cent of the total who could be served by an Alberta to Montreal pipe line.
Unless the government has information not available to the market surveyor or this house concerning very large additional markets for gas north of lake Superior, this question must be raised:	Does the serving
of less than 4-J per cent of the potential market and 2 per cent of the potential consumers justify the expanding of two score or more extra millions of dollars? Such extra cost, we must remember, would have


to be borne by gas producers and their provincial government partners through lower wellhead values; by consumers with particular emphasis on the householder consumer; and probably also by the taxpayers generally through some form of subsidy.
Would not one of the following routes better serve Canada as a whole in view of their lower cost and sounder economies? One, from Alberta across Saskatchewan and Manitoba, swinging south of lake Superior across northern Michigan, re-entering Canada at Sault Ste. Marie, thence to Sudbury and south to Toronto, then branching east to Montreal and Ottawa and west into southern Ontario, serving all communities along the route; or in lieu of that, the same route across western Canada and north Michigan, but branching at Mackinac strait, with a branch swinging east to serve the Sault Ste. Marie and Sudbury areas and the main line swinging south across Michigan to re-enter Canada near Sarnia, thence moving east through southern Ontario to Toronto, Ottawa Montreal and other communities. Or, three, either of these two routes to eastern Canada, coupled with a branch-off to Minneapolis-St. Paul, where a market for 35 to 50 billion cubic feet yearly would be immediately available with an existing utility company, to absorb surplus gas from Alberta during the five years or more that would be required to build up markets in eastern Canada.
Each of these alternatives offers benefits to Canadian consumers greater than would be obtained from a line north of the lakes. This is particularly true for consumers on the prairies and, if the Sarnia route is used, the consumers in southern Ontario, who would be brought nearer, in cost-distance, to the west's gas.
The supply provinces, Alberta and Saskatchewan, would reap the benefits of better wellhead gas prices, aiding their economies directly through improved government revenue from gas sales, and increased incentive for continued large-scale exploration for more oil and gas in the west.
I am not unmindful of the lakehead cities. I trust their potential market would prove sufficient to justify construction of a branch pipe line from any main line that might be built to eastern Canada.
In conclusion, the Alberta conservation board will commence hearings May 11 on applications to move gas westward from that province. It is likely that the hearings will include much evidence on the economic and engineering aspects of all proposed pipe-line routes and markets. The studies by that board will be in line with the policy recently

stated by Premier Manning, a policy with which as an Albertan I fully agree. He said:
In approving the export of surplus gas, the government will adhere to its policy of giving first priority to other Canadian markets if, in the opinion of the conservation board, the economic factors involved are not incompatible with the interests of Alberta producers and the province as a whole.
I trust that this Ottawa government will make it possible for the board of transport commissioners to make a full and complete study of all possible routes for gas, by not binding that board to consideration only of applications for pipe-line construction along routes entirely on Canadian territory.
Between Alberta's conservation board and Canada's transport board our nation has the opportunity to obtain from impartial studies the answers to the vital questions concerning natural gas supply for eastern Canadians and utilization of the west's gas resources in the manner best calculated to serve Canada's interests.
I trust that opportunity will not be lost because of emotional appeals or mere political considerations that could prevent full impartial studies, by tying in advance the hands of the investigators, the board of transport commissioners.

That sub-clause (a) of clause 6 of this bill be amended by deleting the words "or outside" in line 14; by deleting the words "and/or international" in line 19; by deleting the words "the main" and "line or" in line 26, and by inserting after the word "that" in line 26 thereof the word "all".
The effect of this amendment, on being adopted and forwarded, was that the bill now before us would provide for a pipe line entirely within Canada to the east. That is what we were actually considering. I believe it is appropriate that we should bear in mind that this amendment has a considerable effect and that we should have due regard to what is actually before us in that respect.
The question as to whether the company which will be incorporated by this bill, if the bill is passed by the house, or any other corporation would obtain a licence from the board of transport commissioners when the time comes for them to make their application and have it considered, is not actually in issue before us at this time. I think, however, it is appropriate that certain comments be made in regard to this subject when we bear in mind the fact that the bill now before us relates only to a line entirely within Canada.

The question before us is not whether it is wise for the province of Alberta to permit the export of gas from that province. That is something which is under the control of the government of the province of Alberta. It has been stated by the premier of that province that the Alberta government has decided that it is their intention to permit the export of gas. We are therefore not called upon to argue the merits or otherwise of such a proposal from the point of view of the residents of Alberta. There are those who think that the people of Alberta would be wise to insist that the natural gas produced in that province be entirely used for the residents of that province. Again I emphasize the fact that this subject does not come before us for consideration. The government of Alberta has taken its position in this respect.
The question before us is as to what happens after the gas leaves Alberta. That question does fall within the authority of a tribunal which has been set up for the purpose of considering applications for permission to handle natural gas. As far as we are concerned at the moment, we are dealing with an application for incorporation which contains the provision that the pipe line shall run east from Alberta entirely within the boundaries of Canada.
I realize that in considering this subject it is natural that the point of view should be shaped in some measure by the part of Canada in which we live and also by the experience any of us may have had with regard to matters of this kind. However I think there has been one clearly expressed purpose-and may I say that the purpose has been expressed from both sides of the house-namely that it is the best interests of Canadians which should be considered in dealing with a question of this kind.
Our party has put on record consistently its belief that in the use of natural gas, as in the case of other resources, the legitimate self-interest of Canadians should be the first consideration of the representatives of the people of Canada who meet in the House of Commons. At no time has the assertion of that simple but understandable policy been intended to convey-nor, I suggest, could it properly have conveyed-any demand that there should be no export to the United States of either natural gas or other resources where it was consistent with our legitimate self-interest that this should be done.
I agree that economic factors must be given consideration. It would be folly to deny that cost and the other economic factors related to any operation of this kind should be carefully examined in deciding whether

The Royal Assent
it is wise to have a pipe line of this kind entirely within Canada.
The history of dealings betweeen Canada and the United States is one of friendly exchange of resources where that exchange is to the common advantage of both countries. We have had unhappy experiences; and I have no doubt there have been occasions when the people of the United States as well thought we might have done something more favourable to them. Nevertheless, on the whole the relationship between these two countries has been one that may be regarded with admiration by everyone living here or elsewhere.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock. EXCISE TAX ACT
The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Abbott for the second reading
Excise Tax Act
of Bill No. 225, to amend the Excise Tax Act, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Drew.
(Translation):

Mr. Speaker, I wish to conclude the remarks I was making this afternoon on this very important matter of the sales tax imposed on municipalities.
Our municipalities are faced with enormous problems. In most cities and towns municipalities are requested to increase the various services and I think it is absolutely illogical for the federal government to impose that tax on purchases paid for out of funds derived from property owners.
All of which means that our taxation system in Canada should be revised, so as to put an end to the discussion that has been going on for several years regarding the delimitation of the various taxation powers and give back to our three levels of government the sources of revenue they need for their administration. In my opinion the time is ripe, more than ever before, for the federal government to abandon its centralizing policy and convene, as soon as possible, a federal-provincial conference where the whole taxation problem could be settled once and for all from the federal, provincial and municipal aspects, so as to alleviate the burden of small property owners and encourage Canadians, and more particularly our young people, to become home owners and thus ensure the prosperity of Canada, a country where real estate is one of the mainstays.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words only on a particular point. The hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) stated this afternoon that the municipalities of the province of Quebec are the most seriously affected by the federal sales tax on their purchases.
The hon. member for Three Rivers gave no reason to justify such a statement. However, Mr. Speaker, I wish to point out to this house one reason that I found myself, and it is that, in the province of Quebec, both municipalities and school boards must pay the provincial sales tax.
As all the hon. members know, I am sure, the people of Quebec pay a provincial sales tax. Well then, neither the municipalities nor the school boards of the province of Quebec are exempted from this provincial sales tax on their purchases. If the hon. member for Three Rivers is right when he says that it is not logical for the federal government to

Excise Tax Act
impose a sales tax on purchases made bymunicipalities, it is much more illogical for a mother to impose a sales tax on her own children.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext:
Before putting the question I will hear any hon. members who would like to speak to the point of order.
I might say that this afternoon I raised the point of order because, in the first place, I questioned whether the amendment was relevant to the bill. There is also another point that strikes me, and that is whether the amendment does not attach conditions to the passing of second reading of the bill.
The amendment reads:
That Bill No. 225 be not now read the second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house consideration should be given to the introduction of legislation which would provide for the exemption of all municipal councils and school boards from the payment of excise taxes . . .
et cetera. It occurs to me that either the amendment is a negative of the motion for second reading and sets forth a different proposal not contemplated in the bill or it attaches conditions to the second reading of the bill. I am prepared to make my ruling or to hear hon. members if they would like to speak to the question of whether or not the motion is in order.
In my opinion the amendment is out of order for the reason that it is either a negative of the motion for the second reading of the bill and sets forth a different proposal not contemplated in the bill, or it approves the second reading of the bill with certain conditions attached. The latter part is without doubt irregular and, for the reasons which I have mentioned, I rule the amendment out of order.

Mr. Speaker, as I understand it one of your reasons, if not the chief reason, for ruling the amendment out of order is the last part of the amendment. I propose now to move an amendment which will be free from that difficulty and which I hope Your Honour will find satisfactory. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green):
That Bill No. 225 be not now read the second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house consideration should be given to the introduction of legislation which would provide for the exemption of all municipal councils and school boards from the payment of excise taxes, including the 10 per cent sales tax. on all their purchases of machinery and other equipment.
I want to make a few brief comments, Mr. Speaker. I noted particularly that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) said he did not think it was desirable for the federal treasury
[Mr. Lesage.l
to take direct action in respect of the financial position of the municipalities. I think I understand the point he has in mind. But the point he is discussing there is the taking of action in the sense of meddling or interfering with the finances of the municipality. This seems to me to be an entirely different matter. This proposal is merely to relieve them. It is not a question of interfering, except the kind of interference that we all like very much when it happens.
One thing the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) said this afternoon which I think it relevant to repeat, and which I should like to stress for a moment, is the position with regard to education. The federal government has dealt generously with education at the top level, and has given great relief to many of the universities who are in great need of it. But at the lower end of the scale we all know the accumulating difficulties which are facing school boards, and the tremendous rise in the cost of education.
Whether or not we should make education such an expensive thing I shall not pause to discuss now. We have done it. It is a tremendous problem for the municipalities, and I am thinking particularly of the school boards. For that reason it seems to me that the relief which is here proposed is something which would be of great benefit to the community. We, of course, in this party have advocated a general lowering of the sales tax for reasons which I do not need to repeat. I suggest that this is a particular area in which relief might be given which would pay off thirty, sixty or one hundredfold in respect of the assistance which would be given to hard-pressed municipalities and perhaps to still harder-pressed school boards.

When I spoke on the budget
debate, Mr. Speaker, I pointed out to the minister and the house that in the building of the Granville street bridge the city of Vancouver is paying to the dominion government between $500,000 and $600,000 by way of sales tax on the materials going into that bridge. One has only to compare that fact with the fact that if an individual were building a $16-5 million office building in Vancouver most of the material going into that building would be free of sales tax. That is because of the exemption contained in that portion of schedule III to the act which concerns the group of materials which are described as "certain building materials". One of those items is structural steel to be used exclusively for the framework and support of buildings. This exemption would apply, therefore, in the case of a building but does not apply in the case of structural steel used for a bridge.

I do not know how that situation can best be remedied, whether it should be done by a change in the schedule to the act or whether there should be some exemption for municipalities written into the body of the Excise Tax Act. However, I wish to point out to the minister that that is a very unfair situation.
The money which is being paid by the city in sales tax on the materials used in the bridge is raised largely by levies on the homes of the residents in that city. It is sufficiently onerous for them to have to build the bridge without adding another $500,000 or $600,000 by way of sales tax.
I realize that the situation is a difficult one. It is not as simple as it looks on the surface, but I do urge upon the minister that some steps be taken at this session to relieve the municipalities from the need of paying sales tax on such expenditures as for the materials for a bridge or public works within their own boundaries. I do not think a very good case could be made out for making home owners pay a sales tax under those conditions.

Mr. Speaker, we have been considering this afternoon the toll taken of the hard-pressed municipalities by the federal government in the form of sales and excise taxes. We have been considering the extent to which these exactions impose upon the municipalities burdens which it is grossly unfair that the federal government should impose. We have been considering the heavy and growing burdens that the municipalities have been called upon to bear. Indeed the weight of responsibility that has been cast upon the municipalities has been literally growing by leaps and bounds as social services have multiplied, as educational facilities have been extended, as housing burdens have been passed on to an increasingly greater degree to municipal governments.
The total incidence of these burdens has resulted in a situation where the municipalities are today literally overwhelmed. At the same time they have been called upon, apart from such assistance as has been afforded to them by the provincial governments, to function with the same limited tax base that was given to them 85 years ago, when their burdens were infinitely less than they are today. The time has long passed when there should be a fundamental review of the whole question of tax burdens and administrative responsibilities as between the different levels of government in this country.
We of the opposition have today properly pointed out how unfair it is for the federal government, when virtually asserting that with only one slight modification it shall have full exemption from taxation by the provinces and the municipalities on federal property, to impose burdens upon the municipalities in the form of taxation. If this taxation were imposed upon the municipalities by means of a direct levy, open and visible, then many people in this country, who may not be as fully aware of this problem as are those who bear responsibilities

Excise Tax Act
for municipal government, would indeed be shocked. Yet just as onerous a burden is being cast upon the municipalities by the federal government today in this indirect and hidden form.
This form of indirect imposition is all the more onerous because it is levied not on the end consumer but upon the manufacturer or producer. In previous debates we have been shown how this tax levied at the manufacturing or producing level goes on attracting to itself mark-ups, and mark-ups on mark-ups, and mark-ups on mark-ups on mark-ups, as it passes from the hands of the manufacturer to the wholesaler, to the jobber, to the retailer, and finally to the consumer.
This 10 per cent sales tax levy is costing the municipalities not 10 per cent but about 20 per cent on an average. The federal government derives a benefit of 10 per cent and the rest is distributed along the line among those through whose hands the goods have passed before they eventually reach the hands of the municipalities. This form of taxation upon the municipalities is in that respect much more burdensome and more reprehensible than would be a direct tax levied upon the municipalities by the federal government.
Among all the anomalies, among all the injustices in the federal tax structure today that are simply crying out for reform there is none more pressing than the one we have been discussing here today of this iniquitous imposition by the federal government upon the municipalities.
There is one other form of imposition by way of excise and sales taxes that the federal government is levying today which I think ought to be commented upon at this stage of the proceedings. I refer to the extent to which social welfare agencies, which are doing such admirable work in all parts of this country, are being taxed by the federal government through these sales and excise taxes. This has been the subject matter of representations to the federal government, but apparently they have not been effective in winning support from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) or his associates.
Three years ago you will recall that this house did legislate limited relief for certain types of institutions of a charitable nature. By. chapter 15, section 6 of the statutes of 1950 a new section 105A was added to the Excise Tax Act. The effect of that useful and commendable amendment is that institutions of the nature described in the section were permitted, where they purchased goods for their own use and not for resale, to make

application to the minister for the refund of an amount equal to the tax paid. The class of institution which was permitted to enjoy this right was described in the following words:
(a)	a bona fide public institution whose principal purpose is to provide permanent or semi-permanent shelter and care for children or aged, infirm or incapacitated persons who reside in the institution; and
(b)	in receipt annually of aid from the government of Canada or a province for the maintenance of persons specified in paragraph (a).
It will be seen that in the amendment of 1950 parliament gave recognition, although limited, to the principle that institutions engaged in social welfare work coming within certain definitions should not be subject to the payment of federal excise or sales taxes, and that where they purchased goods subject to those taxes and paid the tax, they should be entitled to make application to the minister for a refund of an amount equivalent to the tax paid. In my submission that limited recognition of principle should be extended.
There are many welfare agencies in this country whose work on behalf of the people is simply invaluable but which do not qualify within this definition of institutions. They do not give institutional care of the kind mentioned in section 105A. Indeed, many of the social welfare agencies which are members of community chests in all our cities and larger communities in Canada are without any status under this section and are being subjected to federal taxation. It would shock the conscience of many people, Mr. Speaker, were they aware of this fact, to know that the federal government is taxing charitable organizations engaged in social welfare work. You go to the average citizen in the street and tell him that the federal government is imposing federal taxes upon social welfare agencies engaged in purely altruistic work and you will, in my belief, shock his conscience. The fact of the matter is that this is going on year after year right under our noses; and notwithstanding that representations based upon very solid considerations have been submitted to the government, the government so far has turned a deaf ear.
May I remind the house that these groups which do not enjoy any of this benefit today are very large and important ones. Take all the welfare agencies, for instance, that are engaged in the prevention of individual and family breakdowns, that are engaged in work that saves the public treasury at all levels of government a great deal of money. Among the various classes of welfare agencies that do not qualify under the definition are

many children's aid societies, family welfare bureaux, visiting nurse associations, community chests and welfare councils.
How extensive is the problem, Mr. Speaker? The Canadian welfare council recently conducted an inquiry, and they obtained returns from community chest and welfare associations throughout the country. Based upon that investigation they came to the conclusion that in the year past these welfare agencies purchased goods which were subject to sales tax-I am eliminating entirely all goods that were purchased free of sales tax-to the value of $2,149,000. They also estimated that the sales tax cost them approximately $506,000; and here we have to take account of the fact that mark-ups were included on many of these goods as they passed from hand to hand before they eventually reached the consumer, in this case the welfare agencies.
Perhaps it is just a little unfortunate that this tax does not take the form of a direct, open, visible levy by the federal government on these welfare agencies. Then the public would become aware of the iniquity of the federal imposition of taxes upon social welfare agencies. But again the problem is in the same position entirely as the federal imposition of tax upon municipalities. It is hidden, it is indirect, and the public is not aware of the extent or nature, or indeed of the fact, of these impositions.
I appreciate that there are administrative difficulties involved. I am not saying the problem can be reduced to such simple proportions that, by the mere changing of a word or two in the act, the end result which is so desirable can be brought about. But I am satisfied that if the intelligence and ingenuity of the government and its advisers were applied to the problem, with a recognition of the fact that it is fundamentally wrong that the federal government should tax welfare agencies, the problem could be resolved in a very short space of time. I appeal to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). I know the problem is not new to him. I know that mine is by no means the first appeal that has been made to him.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was being made back in Mr. Bennett's day.

I do not recall when the first appeal was made in the house, but I urge the minister to undertake a study of the problem with a much more favourable approach to it than, he has demonstrated in the past. I am informed that he has had extensive briefs on the subject, and I have no doubt that he has studied them. I have no doubt also that he has been concerned about what
Excise Tax Act
may be regarded as certain administrative problems that this question involves.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a euphemistic way of putting it-yes.

But I am satisfied that if the minister will apply to this problem the same ingenuity that he has applied to some other questions, and will follow the methods by which he has endeavoured to treat certain other problems, this problem is by no means impossible of solution. We have had a recognition of the principle in section 105A. To that extent the federal government and parliament have recognized that it is fundamentally wrong-I go further and say that it is iniquitous-that the federal government should be taxing social welfare agencies engaged in purely philanthropic work. I urge with all the earnestness at my command that the government take this problem in hand, and that without further delay the Minister of Finance undertake the redress of a situation which, in my humble opinion, if brought home to the man in the street would shock his conscience to its foundations.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a word with respect to this matter because, while the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) expressed our view very well and very forcibly and made a plea to the minister for the removal of this tax from municipalities and social welfare agencies, I want to say something about the tax itself. As has already been said, when the 10 per cent tax, 2 per cent of which we of course understand now goes for social security, reaches the ultimate consumer it has been pyramided to 15 per cent, 16 per cent or even-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think experience justifies that, but it is a matter of assertion on both sides. My information is that is not the case.
Suppose we leave it that the tax is pyramided, without mentioning any figures.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not even prepared to concede that, but my hon. friend can make his argument.

The minister will not disagree with that, so we will leave out the figures. In that sense it is a tax imposed by the federal government which, when it is finally paid, involves an imposition greater than the tax, whatever the extent may be; and I am not going to argue about that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In a highly competitive business it is pretty modest.

To that extent I say the tax is bad in any event.

Excise Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is true of corporate income tax, too; any indirect tax; customs duties.
If levied at the manufacturer's level.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is where the corporation tax is levied in most cases.

As a rule an indirect tax of this description is pyramided. If it is the corporation tax and the corporation levies it upon the public then by the time the public pays it, it is probably more than the tax imposed by the government. There is no disagreement between the minister and ourselves that a tax of this description, when paid by the consumer, is usually higher than the amount imposed by the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not necessarily.

I said "usually". I qualified it. I said "usually" and the minister says "not necessarily". I think we mean the same thing in that respect. What I say is that when this was first imposed the public of Canada regarded it as a tax that was not a good tax. Indeed, when my hon. friends in the Liberal party left office in 1930, as I remember it there was a 1 per cent sales tax. Then the Progressive Conservatives came into power.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The Liberal Conservatives.
Well, the Conservatives came into power and they increased the tax to 4 per cent.
Oh?
And what did the Liberal opposition say of it at that time?
They raised Cain.
I did not say that, but I think that is a very adequate way of putting it.

Mr. King said it was
"iniquitous".

The great Canadian who subsequently became minister of finance, Hon. J. L. Ralston, opposed it strenuously. On June 4, 1931, speaking in this house and protesting the increase from 1 per cent to 4 per cent, Mr. Ralston said this:
It is the ordinary, everyday consumers, the men and women who are hard put to make ends meet-
That was at that time, of course.

men who are out of work, who are now called upon to pay the extra amount in connection with the sales tax.
They are the ones who are the hardest hit. There were many out of work at that time and, of course, there are some people out of work now. There are people living on old age pensions and there are people who are

maintaining homes on small wages and incomes. The sales tax reaches right into the homes of our people. It applies on articles of clothing, furniture, and a long list that I am not going to put on the record because it has been put on the record before; but there is a long list of essential commodities of life which are subject to this sales tax. As I say, there was never a truer indictment of this tax than was made on June 4, 1931, by the Hon. J. L. Ralston when he was speaking on behalf of the Liberal party in this house.
Then I remember the election of 1935; I was a candidate, and I was elected at that time. I remember that the Liberal candidates across the country paid particular attention to the sales tax. I remember too a broadcast made by the leader of the opposition of the day in which he criticized the sales tax. We thought, although we were never quite sure what the then leader of the Liberal party meant when he spoke, that if they were elected they were going to do away with that sales tax. Instead of that they raised it to 6 per cent; and then it was raised to 8 per cent.

For whatever purpose the tax is used, it is not a good tax. It is a regressive tax.
I personally believe that the sales tax is one of the poorest forms of taxation that we have. It is a hidden tax which people do not know they are paying; and a tax which is levied on many of the essential commodities of life at a time when the cost of living is high. It is oppressive on many families and on pensioners with small incomes. This tax takes from them a very great deal in their contributions to Canada.
It might be said that everyone should pay taxes. Well, I will not disagree with that statement except to say that if people pay taxes they should at least know they are paying them and know what they are paying in the form of taxation. Therefore I want to-

support what my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) had to say on our behalf this afternoon, and to appeal to the minister to consider the representations that have been made (a) to remove the tax from municipalities and (b) to remove the tax from these social and welfare organizations.
As far as municipalities are concerned today their burdens are heavy, and one of the great burdens, of course, is the burden of education. The government refuses to make grants to the provinces for the purpose of education, and I think an attempt at least should be made to relieve the burden on municipalities in connection with this tax.
Mr. Speaker, I just want to make that appeal to the minister for a reconsideration of the proposals he has made to this house in this regard.

Mr. Speaker, I want to support those who have been urging the exemption of municipalities from the sales tax on municipal purchases. I am not as sure as some of the members are that the minister will not listen to this appeal. In his budget the minister has shown some interest in the municipalities. In his revision of the income tax he has at least brought the municipalities in line with provincial governments and with the federal government in the matter of elected representatives and has made provision whereby their expenses may be deducted for income tax purposes. That would seem to indicate that the minister is showing some concern for the municipalities, and I think it is not an impossibility that even at this hour the minister may consider the justness of the appeal that has been made at the present time.
The minister has been quite concerned over the question of double taxation for corporations. I wonder if he has taken into consideration the extent to which this sales tax, levied upon municipal purchases, is a double tax in so far as property taxpayers within the municipality are concerned. The sales tax is collected on municipal purchases, and the home owners are the people who pay municipal taxes. They are also the people who pay these indirect taxes, just as every other Canadian pays them.
In addition to the sales tax which the ordinary home owner in the city pays together with every other Canadian citizen, he pays an extra sales tax when he has to support the municipal government, because the municipal government has to raise money with which to reimburse the federal government for the sales tax. There is a phase of double taxation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not double taxation at all; it is just the opposite.

It is just as clear a case of double taxation as it is in the case of corporations, with which the minister is very much concerned. I know the minister does not see it that way; but the home owner in the city, who bears municipal taxes, pays his ordinary sales taxes to the federal government the same as the rest of us do. In addition he pays, through his real estate tax and through taxes on his home, an additional sales tax to the government because the municipality has to pay taxes on its municipal purchases.
There is another point I would like to call to the minister's attention. While our municipalities are creatures of the province, and while the minister may say that it is the business of the provincial governments to bring relief to the municipalities, the cost of municipal government today is in no small measure due to federal government policies. Municipal taxes have increased within recent years because of inflation, and inflation is the direct result of the policy pursued by this government. The government could, had it desired, have checked inflation after the war just as it checked inflation during the war years. It chose to let inflation run, probably not wild but wild to some extent at least. It was the government's deliberate policy to take off all controls, so the government must bear some responsibility for inflation which has brought an extra burden to bear upon the home owners who pay taxes within the municipalities.
Then the increased industrialization, from which the federal government has obtained great benefit and for which the federal government takes credit, has affected the urban municipalities, and particularly the urban population. Within the ten years since the previous census was taken the urban population increased about 24 per cent. This influx is due directly to industrialization, for which as I said the government takes great credit and from which the government derives great benefit by way of taxes. This industrialization has thrown an extra burden upon the municipalities. As a result also of the government's immigration policy there has been a further influx of population into our urban centres. The government brings thousands of people into this country, presumably as agricultural workers, and they are supposed to stay on the farms. Before they are in this country more than a few months we find them back in the cities. I say that on each of these counts the federal government should, in my opinion, assume some responsibility for the extra

Excise Tax Act
burden which in recent years has been thrust upon the municipalities.
It is true that the exemption of purchases by municipalities from the sales tax will reduce federal revenues. It should be much easier, though, for the federal government to make up the difference than it is for the municipalities to bear the extra burden which inflation, and in the case of urban centres immigration, has thrown upon them.
Today we have a serious housing situation in the urban centres. One of the greatest difficulties confronted in the building of homes is that people cannot afford to build even moderately priced homes because of the increased taxation which education by itself will throw upon the municipality. This government is unwilling to bear any share of the cost of education at the elementary or secondary school level. Here is an opportunity, by following the precedent the minister set in the matter of elected employees of the municipalities and their income, for the government to bring some relief to the municipalities by exempting them from these taxes.
I am quite sure that the Canadian people as a whole, even though they might be called upon to bear the same amount of over-all taxes were such exemptions granted, would rather see the federal government grant those exemptions and make up the resultant loss in revenue by other means at the disposal of the federal government. They do not wish to continue to impose this burden upon the home owners of this country.

Mr. Speaker, my colleagues and I have, upon many occasions, registered our opposition to hidden taxes. We have had very definite reasons for doing that, and I need not take very long in order to recount some of those reasons.
In the first place we have condemned hidden taxes, the sales tax and excise tax, inasmuch as they do not in any sense bear a relationship to ability to pay. The poorest person in the land finds the cost of many of his essentials inflated purely as a consequence of hidden taxes. We have condemned these taxes because of what was so well stated by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), namely that you find yourself paying taxes upon taxes-in my opinion a bad principle, a dangerous procedure. We have condemned these taxes because of the fact that they are an extremely important factor in causing inflation, in causing prices even today to remain at extremely high levels. Because of 
these hidden taxes, many of the things which should properly be in the category of necessities have now become luxuries. In fact it .was only a short while ago that I read this. The question was asked, what is a luxury? The answer was, a luxury is a necessity plus Abbott's taxes. I think that in some respects there is a lot of truth to that assertion.
I was rather astounded to read only today that in 1952 the wages paid in the automobile industry approximated $131 million, but that sales and excise taxes exceeded that amount by almost $6 [DOT] 5 million. To me that was a most astonishing revelation, provided, of course, that the figures are correct; and I have no reason for assuming that they are not. In other words when people talk so glibly about high wages being such an important part of the high cost of motor vehicles, they should bear in mind that approximately $137 million in taxes was taken out of that industry or charged to the purchasers of motor vehicles in the year 1952. There is one matter about which I desire further information. I understand it is customary for the motor manufacturers to have suppliers of parts for these vehicles. Are sales and excise taxes paid on the parts that go into the automobile, and then is sales tax imposed upon the final product? In that case it would mean the imposition of a double sales tax.
I think I know, Mr. Speaker, why certain governments cling so tenaciously to that hidden tax. They are less likely to be blamed for what they are actually doing. All too frequently a purchaser will blame the retailer for the high price which is made up in a substantial part of hidden taxes, or he will blame the wholesaler or the manufacturer and say that they are responsible for the higher prices. Governments resist removing these hidden taxes.
For these and other reasons we again take very strong exception to these hidden taxes. When speaking in the house on March 2, I believe it was, I raised the question of the taxes which are imposed upon municipal purchases. It is rather an interesting thing, Mr. Speaker. There was a time when the opposition of the Minister of Finance to making this concession was the necessity for revenue. That argument was laboured, and possibly at the time it was laboured it was a rather difficult one to counter by one's argument then. Of course that argument has lost much of its validity and we are now faced with the argument that it would be extremely difficult to administer. It has been pointed out, for example, that in the United States it is being done. Concessions are made to the states by the national government as far as state purchases are concerned. There

has been no insurmountable obstacle facing them as far as administration is concerned.
Now that argument has become less valid, so the minister labours the fact that he does not believe we should reach down and deal with creatures of the provincial governments. They may be creatures of the provincial governments but they are also definitely victims of the federal government, because after all federal government policy has its repercussions even in the municipalities.
One need not labour the problems with which the municipalities are confronted. We recognize fully that right across this country the provincial governments have been going farther and farther in their attempts to relieve the burden borne by the municipalities, and they have been doing a good deal in many instances in helping to remove that burden. But certainly one of the most effective ways of helping them through their difficulties would be by the federal government foing for the municipal governments what they now do for the provincial governments. As I pointed out before, the municipal government is a legislative body exercising authority granted to it under the municipal act, and n its sphere carrying on a public service n the same way that the provincial government carries it on in the wider sphere, and n the same way that the federal government carries on its responsibilities within its iphere of jurisdiction.
One could take more time, but my purpose s not just to take time. On behalf of my colleagues I again wish to register strenuous Ejection to these hidden taxes. Certain >f them should be removed completely md others should be reduced. We also go >n record as urging the federal government o give careful consideration to these requests if the municipal governments that the sales md excise taxes be removed on the commodities they purchase.

Therefore without blaming the minister at all for many of the things that have happened, for inflation and all that sort of thing, over which this government may have some control but which in some respects at least is a part of the world-wide condition over which no government has complete control, I suggest to the minister that he reconsider this matter. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to take only a very few minutes. This afternoon I gave, rather too briefly perhaps, the reasons which actuated the government in feeling that it could not recommend for the municipalities an exemption from the imposition of the sales tax. My friend the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) suggested this evening that this was in fact imposing a double tax. Of course that is not the case.
I tried to point out this afternoon that I could see no reason why, in a tax which is payable by individuals on the purchase of commodities, they should be relieved of that tax because they are purchased through a corporation, in this case a municipal corporation. In fact, if municipalities were exempt from the payment of this sales tax it would be necessary to make up the revenue somewhere else, and it would have to be done by increasing some tax or increasing the rate of tax and imposing it on people who are in fact the same people because everybody resides in a municipality. I say that because, of course, it is not in fact a double tax.
I know there has been a great deal of talk about the sales tax. This debate this evening has almost developed into our annual debate on the evils of the sales tax. I have dealt with that matter before. I have endeavoured to show that, with the wide list of exemptions-in the case of the small income man nearly two-thirds of his purchases being exempt from the sales tax- this is not a regressive tax. We get from the tax, or I estimate that we shall get from the sales tax this year, about $590 million. If that revenue is to be forgone, we must get it somewhere else. We could get it by increasing the personal income tax on the average by about 50 per cent; and I know that would be an extremely popular method with my friend the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) who is a strong opponent of the sales tax. We could get it perhaps by increasing the corporation tax further. But let me hasten to say here, to those who oppose hidden taxes, that the corporation tax is today our greatest hidden tax and produces substantially more than the sales tax produces.
I know that it is the job of people in the opposition to oppose taxes. My friend the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well) cited Mr. Ralston's denunciation of the
[Mr. Maclnnis.l
sales tax in 1931. I venture to say that if he were sitting on your right hand, Mr. Speaker, or if my friend the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) were sitting on your right hand, he would be defending the sales tax just exactly as I am doing this evening. In my opinion-and I have said this before -with the steeply progressive personal income tax that we have and with the heavy corporation taxes that we have, the general sales tax with the list of exemptions which we have now developed is a perfectly fair and equitable tax.
Reference was made to 1935. My recollection is that in 1935 we obtained 23 per cent of our revenues from direct taxes and 77 per cent from indirect taxes and in other ways. This year we estimate that we shall obtain 57-5 per cent or thereabouts of our revenues from direct taxes and about 33 or 34 per cent from indirect taxes. I therefore think it is fair to say that there has been a recasting of our tax structure which has made it, in my judgment, much more equitable than was the tax structure which existed ten or fifteen years ago.
We have much heavier obligations. Nearly 25 per cent of our total budget goes in the form of social security payments of one sort and another to our people. Those are transfer payments, and the moneys have to be raised by taxation. As I say, anyone who occupies the position that I occupy and who forgoes revenue from the sales tax must get that revenue from somewhere else. I have heard no suggestions made in this house that the rate of personal income tax was too low, or that the rate of corporation tax was too low, or that the special excise tax rate was too low, or that the rate of tax on cigarettes was too low, or even that the rate of tax on liquor was too low. So let us face the fact that if we are going to remove some of these taxes we have to be prepared to put them on somewhere else.
I do not like to do unpleasant things any more than anybody else. I should be exceedingly happy personally to accede to this widespread demand and request that the municipalities should be exempt from the sales tax. But as I pointed out this afternoon, that would involve a very substantial loss of revenue which would have to be made up somewhere else. It would involve serious administrative difficulties, and I am using a euphemism when I say that. It would involve serious administrative difficulties to see that it was fully and fairly administered over the approximately four thousand municipalities in Canada. In my judgment one of the tests of a good tax is that it should be fully, thoroughly and efficiently administered. Sc

far as I am concerned I came to the conclusion, after most careful consideration, that it would not be appropriate that this exemption should be made.

In the first place I call attention to the note with respect to clause 11. My understanding is that clause 11 really does extend the scope of the tax to some considerable extent, but I will come back to that in a moment.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No, it does not extend it. It just divides it. There is merely a division and a clarification, in order that we may know exactly what proportion of the tax comes from radio and what proportion comes from television, and that is for the purpose of statistics.

The parliamentary assistant is repeating what is in the note on the right hand side of the page, but I think the note perhaps does not take the opposition fully into the government's confidence. What I want to point out is that so far as I can see there is an extension of the tax. The matter is well set out in a dispatch from the Winnipeg Free Press which confirms information that I myself got elsewhere, and I shall read this extract.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. As the hon. member knows, in committee remarks must be strictly relevant to the clause, and it is not in order to read long extracts from newspapers.
Mr. Chairman, this extract sets out the argument which I wish to make. If you wish me to do it in my own words-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would be much better.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I cannot allow the hon. member to read such extracts.

All right, Mr. Chairman. My understanding is that the section as now written covers certain things, wired music operations, community antenna operations and piped operations such as used by a company called Rediffusion Incorporated in Montreal, which operation has been before the tariff board. The company argued that it was not included under the words "telecast receiving units" and on February 17 the tariff board upheld their appeal. I submit we now have an act which, by reason of the extension of the wording, is going to make quite sure that the appeal board does not go astray and confirm the

Excise Tax Act
ruling already given, which is that these particular articles are not taxable. That is what I mean by saying that I think the scope of the section is widened, and that is what I mean by saying that I think the last sentence of the explanation is, to use an admirable word which the Minister of Finance has used twice already, a euphemism.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is a very polite word.

The last
sentence in the descriptive note reads as follows:
The item has been further clarified by using more descriptive terms.
That is a very euphemistic way of saying that the effect of the section has been considerably extended. I think the minister will agree with that. Even he could not be more euphemistic than that. Mr. Chairman, it is ten o'clock. Perhaps I might be given the opportunity to put what I have to say in better shape for tomorrow.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: May I say one word. I agree with what my hon. friend means even if I do not agree with all the words he used, but I cannot agree with him when he says that it extends the meaning of the section. As a matter of fact it clarifies the section to make it certain that the tax applies to all television equipment for programs distributed by any means whatsoever. May I also say that, according to my information, the decision of the tariff board is being appealed from.

If the parliamentary assistant means by clarification that it puts into words what the Department of National Revenue thinks should be the law, if that is his definition of clarification then that is a definition which I do not fully accept.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: We believe it was the intention of the legislators.

May I ask one question. This section, as we followed the statement made by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech, is designed to provide revenue for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. May
I ask in what form provision is to be made to devote to the use of the corporation revenue acquired through the tax imposed by this section?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it the wish of hon. members to carry the section this evening?
No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If not, why not report progress?
Can I have an answer to my question?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is ten o'clock, and hon. members are not ready to pass the section. Why not report progress and ask leave to sit again?
He has the answer all ready, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: There will be a special provision in the Canadian Broadcasting Act.
There will be amendments to that act introduced later this session?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
That is right.
Section stands.
Progress reported.
